articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran Designation Update
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced an Iran Designation Update on November 9, 2026. This action signifies ongoing efforts to target individuals and entities involved in activities deemed detrimental to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests concerning Iran.

Further details regarding the specific individuals or entities designated, and the reasons for their inclusion, are typically provided within the official designation notice. These updates are part of a broader strategy to exert economic pressure on the Iranian regime.
Such designations aim to disrupt financial networks and other support structures that enable Iran's proliferation-sensitive nuclear activities, ballistic missile program, and other malign behaviors.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related Designations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 6, 2026. These actions are part of the ongoing 'Operation Economic Outcast,' which seeks to curtail Iran's ability to fund its military and destabilizing activities.
The designations aim to cripple financial networks that sustain the Iranian regime, targeting individuals and entities that provide support for its various illicit endeavors.
These measures are intended to further restrict Iran's access to the international financial system and disrupt its efforts to evade existing sanctions.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Department of State

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber-Related and Transnational Criminal Organizations; Imposes New Cuba Sanctions
body: On November 5, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting cyber-related and transnational criminal organizations, alongside new sanctions related to Cuba. This action also included the publication of a Cuba-related determination.
The Cuba-related sanctions specifically target a crude oil shipping network, state-owned import and technical-support entities, and China-based suppliers of Cuba's military forces.

These designations are made pursuant to Executive Order 14404, which authorizes sanctions on foreign persons responsible for repression in Cuba and threats to U.S. national security and foreign policy.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Department of State

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Iran-Related Designations, Updates, Alert, and Amended Venezuela GL
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations, updates to certain Iran-related listings, and the publication of an Iran-related OFAC Alert on November 4, 2026.
Concurrently, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a Frequently Asked Question.
The Iran-related actions are part of a broader effort to counter the Iranian regime's illicit activities, including its reliance on false flags for sanctions evasion in its shadow fleet operations.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Department of State

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the issuance of an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026. This amendment modifies existing authorizations concerning transactions involving Iran.

General Licenses are issued by OFAC to authorize certain categories of transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions programs. The specifics of the amendment would detail the scope of the newly authorized activities or changes to previously authorized ones.
Such amendments are often made to fine-tune sanctions policy, respond to evolving geopolitical circumstances, or clarify existing regulations for compliance purposes.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities Related to North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo
body: On October 28, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting entities related to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

These actions are part of ongoing efforts to counter illicit activities that undermine international security and stability, including North Korea's weapons programs and destabilizing actions in the DRC.
The designations aim to disrupt financial networks and support structures enabling these activities, aligning with broader U.S. foreign policy objectives.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / U.S. Department of State

articles.headline: OFAC Reaches Settlement Agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc.
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc. on October 27, 2026. This settlement resolves alleged violations of OFAC sanctions programs.

Settlement agreements typically involve a monetary penalty and a commitment from the company to implement or enhance compliance measures to prevent future violations. The specific details of the violations are outlined in the settlement release.
This action underscores OFAC's continued enforcement efforts to ensure compliance with U.S. sanctions regulations across various industries.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Filing Reports
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) regarding blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC on October 26, 2026. This update aims to provide clearer guidance to U.S. persons and entities on their compliance obligations.

These FAQs are crucial resources for financial institutions and other businesses to understand the nuances of OFAC regulations, particularly concerning how to handle transactions involving sanctioned parties or jurisdictions.
The amendments likely address common questions or areas of confusion, helping to streamline compliance processes and reduce the risk of inadvertent violations.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Iran-Related Designations, Belarus and North Korea Removals, and New General Licenses
body: On October 21, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations. Concurrently, OFAC also announced the removal of certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea.

In addition to these actions, OFAC issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses, along with amended Frequently Asked Questions. These General Licenses authorize specific transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under the respective sanctions programs.
These comprehensive actions reflect OFAC's dynamic approach to sanctions, adjusting measures based on evolving geopolitical landscapes and specific policy objectives.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes PAIPA Designations and Issues Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026. These designations were accompanied by the issuance of associated General Licenses.
The PAIPA designations targeted five Chinese entities over alleged theft of trade secrets related to Google's AI technology.
This marks the second-ever use of PAIPA and its first application against Chinese entities, signaling a strong stance against intellectual property theft.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Fined $1,529,685 by OFAC
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has agreed to pay a civil penalty of $1,529,685 to the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). This settlement resolves alleged violations of OFAC sanctions programs.

The enforcement action highlights OFAC's continued focus on ensuring that companies implement robust compliance programs to prevent unauthorized transactions with sanctioned entities or jurisdictions.
Details of the specific violations leading to this penalty are typically outlined in OFAC's public enforcement release, providing insights into the compliance failures identified.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Assessed $11,662,930 OFAC Penalty

The OFAC settlement addresses apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs, including those related to Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism.
This significant enforcement action underscores the critical importance of comprehensive sanctions compliance programs for financial institutions operating internationally.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Fined $175,015 by OFAC
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics has agreed to pay a civil penalty of $175,015 to the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). This settlement addresses alleged violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

The enforcement action against a logistics company highlights the broad reach of U.S. sanctions and the expectation for all entities involved in international trade and transport to maintain robust compliance measures.
Companies in the logistics sector must exercise due diligence to ensure they are not facilitating transactions that directly or indirectly benefit sanctioned parties or jurisdictions.

articles.headline: Individual Assessed $1,427,230 OFAC Penalty
body: An individual has been assessed a civil penalty of $1,427,230 by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). This enforcement action underscores OFAC's authority to pursue penalties against individuals for sanctions violations.
Individual penalties often arise from direct involvement in prohibited transactions, attempts to circumvent sanctions, or failures to comply with reporting requirements.
This action serves as a reminder that sanctions compliance obligations extend to individuals as well as corporate entities.

The enforcement action against a manufacturing company highlights the importance of sanctions compliance across various industries, even for seemingly routine commercial activities.
Companies must implement effective screening mechanisms and due diligence procedures to ensure that their products and services are not provided to sanctioned parties or destinations.

articles.headline: FTI Consulting, Inc. Pays $1,050,000 OFAC Penalty
body: FTI Consulting, Inc. has paid a civil penalty of $1,050,000 to the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). This settlement addresses alleged violations of OFAC sanctions programs.
Consulting firms, like other service providers, are expected to have robust sanctions compliance programs in place to prevent their services from being used to circumvent U.S. sanctions.
This enforcement action serves as a reminder that professional services, including consulting, can fall under the purview of OFAC regulations if they involve sanctioned entities or activities.

articles.headline: Adani Enterprises Limited Fined $275,000,000 by OFAC

The large fine underscores the critical importance of comprehensive sanctions compliance for major international corporations, particularly those with extensive global operations and supply chains.
This enforcement action highlights OFAC's commitment to holding large entities accountable for sanctions breaches and emphasizes the need for rigorous due diligence and internal controls.

articles.headline: TradeStation Securities, Inc. Pays $1,110,661 OFAC Penalty
body: TradeStation Securities, Inc. has paid a civil penalty of $1,110,661 to the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). This settlement addresses alleged violations of OFAC sanctions programs.

Financial institutions, including brokerage firms, are under strict obligations to prevent transactions that involve sanctioned individuals, entities, or jurisdictions. Failures in screening or monitoring can lead to significant penalties.
This enforcement action reinforces the necessity for robust sanctions compliance programs within the financial services industry to detect and prevent prohibited activities.

articles.headline: Individual Assessed $3,777,000 OFAC Penalty
body: An individual has been assessed a civil penalty of $3,777,000 by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). This substantial penalty highlights OFAC's willingness to pursue significant enforcement actions against individuals who violate sanctions regulations.

Individual liability in sanctions cases can arise from various activities, including facilitating prohibited transactions, engaging in deceptive practices to evade sanctions, or failing to disclose relevant information to OFAC.
This action serves as a strong deterrent, emphasizing that individuals are not immune from severe penalties for sanctions breaches.

articles.headline: IMG Academy, LLC Pays $1,720,000 OFAC Penalty

This enforcement action against an educational and athletic training institution demonstrates that sanctions compliance extends to a wide range of sectors, including those that might not traditionally be considered high-risk.
Organizations in all industries must ensure they have adequate controls in place to prevent interactions with sanctioned individuals, entities, or countries.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
